record_reviews.summary: Oxenden reports finding only five Ophrys arachnites plants after a full day’s search, three flowering, compared with fifty on the same ground two years earlier. He attributes the poor showing to the season and grazing, encloses two flowers, and gives the third to Lady Dundonald. The note is a specimen dispatch with precise seasonal and quantity observations, dated 1862.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1862-05-29; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: G. C. Oxenden is the incoming writer to Darwin; Lady Dundonald is a person Oxenden met and mentions, not a second voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1862 specimen report has no 1851–55 antecedent or response in this packet.

evidence.quote: I hunted some splendid Ground for “Arachnites”, this day—

record_reviews.summary: Oxenden laments Darwin’s move away from orchids, then offers a newly found rich site for Ophrys arachnites and Epipactis palustris. He distinguishes their flowering windows—Epipactis three weeks away, Arachnites at prime—and asks whether Darwin still wants specimens. The emotional opening and practical collection offer are distinct layers of the same incoming note.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1862-06-20; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: G. C. Oxenden is the incoming writer; the remarks about Darwin’s scientific direction are Oxenden’s personal framing, not editorial biography.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1862 orchid offer is outside 1851–55 and no current-period response is identified.

evidence.quote: As a last proof of fidelity, I have just discovered quite a new & rich mine of O. Arachnites

record_reviews.summary: The original Darwin letter is missing. The surviving record is a Ray Society special-council minute dated before 4 November 1864, recording only that a letter from Darwin proposed translating Gärtner’s Bastarderzeugung. The minute is an institutional paraphrase/entry, not Darwin’s full body, and cannot establish the letter’s exact wording or enclosures.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1864-11-03; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: This is a Ray Society minute excerpt reporting a missing C. R. Darwin letter; no individual secretary’s prose or complete Darwin source survives in the record.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Institutional minute replaces the missing Charles Darwin letter; retain unavailable-body status and the 1864 date.

evidence.quote: Read a letter from Mr Darwin suggesting the Translation of Gaertner’s work on “Bastardezeugung”

record_reviews.summary: The original Darwin letter is likewise missing. A Ray Society council minute records that the Society resumed consideration of Gärtner’s translation, read Darwin’s recommendation that the work was not antiquated and needed no valuable added notes, and resolved to accept it for an early year. This is a minute-derived institutional record, not a surviving letter or an exact transcript of Darwin’s argument.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1865-01-06; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The preserved prose is a Ray Society minute reporting C. R. Darwin and Hooker’s recommendations; the absent Darwin letter and the Society’s resolution must remain separate layers.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The minute records an institutional decision and a missing letter, with no 1851–55 source or direct reply.

evidence.quote: a letter from Mr Darwin was read stating that the work was in no degree antiquated

record_reviews.summary: Hensleigh Wedgwood proposes linguistic analogies for Darwin’s species argument: Head/chief and bishop/évêque are more decisive than a long series, and English’s mixed vocabulary resembles geological formations made from earlier continents. He then adds a family travel note about Hartfield and Fanny. The linguistic comparison is the substantive evidence; the family closing does not turn the letter into family news alone.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1857-09-28; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Hensleigh Wedgwood is the incoming writer. The etymological examples and geology analogy are his own reasoning; Darwin’s later use of bishop/évêque is apparatus evidence of knowledge, not a second voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1857 letter is outside 1851–55; its later use in Natural Selection does not backdate contemporary knowledge.

evidence.quote: Head, OE. heved, AS heafod, G. haupt Goth. haubith Lat capit (is) It. capo Fr. chef E. chief.

record_reviews.summary: Wedgwood directly critiques Darwin’s account of moral sense and conscience in Descent. He contrasts the text’s dissatisfaction-from-unsatisfied-instinct explanation with shame arising from another mind’s disapproval, tests the distinction against pointer dogs and baboon rescue/discipline examples, and argues that memory alone cannot recreate the original instinctive dissatisfaction. Darwin’s page references and marginal response notes are separate layers from Wedgwood’s seven-paragraph argument.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1871-03-02; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Hensleigh Wedgwood is the incoming critic; quoted passages from Darwin’s Descent are embedded evidence, while Darwin’s annotations for a later reply are not Wedgwood’s voice.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This is a substantive moral-instinct critique dated 1871, not family news and not an 1851–55 prompt.

evidence.quote: Shame is the true essence of conscience, not resolutions as to one’s future conduct

record_reviews.summary: Buckland says he will arrange Darwin’s visit to see salmon hatching in the Field office window and reports that the Field editor welcomes natural-history queries from practical correspondents. He then lists dubious popular claims—duck/fowl crosses, a viper swallowing its young, dog/fox crosses, and the toad-in-a-hole question—that he has been asked to examine. The note is a mixed editorial invitation and skepticism about reported cases.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1863-01-31; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: F. T. Buckland is the incoming writer; the Field editor’s request and the listed animal stories are reported within Buckland’s body, not independent letters.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1863 Buckland response may answer an unlocated Darwin visit/query, but no specific current-period pair is supported.

evidence.quote: the Editor of The Field requests me to inform you that he would feel much pleased if you would send any natural history Quæries

record_reviews.summary: Buckland compares oyster and fish variation, claims salmon and trout differ by river size, describes making casts rather than stuffed fish, and invites Darwin to the Hampton hatchery. He says he quoted Darwin in a £100,000 salmon-arbitration case, applying Darwin’s limits on unchecked increase, then apologizes for the long report. The practical fishery example and the Darwin quotation are distinct claims.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1864-12-10; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Francis Trevelyan Buckland is the incoming writer; the arbitration parties and hatchery are reported contexts, not additional source voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1864 report is later than the period and does not identify a preserved Darwin response.

evidence.quote: I quoted your book the other day on a Salmon arbitration case

record_reviews.summary: Crocker welcomes Darwin’s proposed Hollyhock and Larkspur experiments, considers repeating Beaton’s Pelargonium test, and describes wild carrots, celery, and beet near Shanklin. He reports an uncertain Linum observation because the plants may have come from cuttings, asks which marsh plants are dimorphous, and admits limited orchid experience. He closes with a broader argument for systematic government or society-funded experiments and a personal health note.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1862-03-12; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: C. W. Crocker is the incoming writer to Darwin; the damaged passages and bracketed restorations remain Crocker’s uncertain testimony, not Darwin’s words.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1862 experimental reply is outside 1851–55; the missing Darwin letter is referenced but not reconstructed.

evidence.quote: I shall have much real enjoyment in trying the experiment upon Hollyhocks.

record_reviews.summary: Daly’s source is a 23-block correction list for Volume 2, with page/line locations and replacements such as ‘berning’ to ‘bearing’, ‘slower’ to ‘more slowly’, and subject-verb corrections. It is an editorial errata document, not a letter body or scientific argument; its numbered blocks must not be collapsed into one short catalogue synopsis.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1868-02-08; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: J. Daly is the source author of the correction memorandum/list; the corrected publication text and any Darwin editorial action are distinct from Daly’s entries.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1868 correction list has no identifiable incoming prompt or Darwin reply in the packet.

evidence.quote: For berning Read bearing

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks carriage-maker John Andrews why his waggonette has not arrived and requests temporary use of a waggonette or phaeton if completion will take another week. The three blocks are a straightforward later commercial logistics note, with no scientific content or implied natural-history question.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1877-03-11; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: C. R. Darwin is the outgoing writer to Andrews; the absent carriage order or Andrews response is not present as a body.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1877 carriage note is a later boundary record; no period relationship is inferred from its administrative subject.

evidence.quote: I have been expecting to receive my waggonette before this time

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Henrietta Litchfield to thank L., keep Spencer’s book, and read twelve pages of his mother’s-hand draft on voice as expression. He calls the passage wretched, points to earlier discussion of screams from pain and antithesis, and asks whether Litchfield and L. find it as poor as he does. This is a draft-review request concerning Expression, not a generic family note.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1871-12-01; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: C. R. Darwin is the sender to H. E. Litchfield; Emma’s handwriting and L./Spencer are referenced layers, not co-authored body voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1871 draft-review request is outside 1851–55 and its missing Litchfield response is not preserved here.

evidence.quote: I wish with all my heart I cd. avoid saying a word on the Voice as a means of Expression

record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s letter to Doubleday resumes a discussion of moth varieties bred from one set of eggs, asks whether they are therefore one species, praises the careful packing of Doubleday’s box, and comments on Peronia colour and size. The opening is visibly truncated, so the precise antecedent and full question are missing; the 1857 date is nevertheless established by related Doubleday letters.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1857-02-04; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: C. R. Darwin is the outgoing writer to Henry Doubleday; Doubleday’s breeding result is referenced as prior input, not present as a separate body here.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1857 exchange is outside the target period and its opening missing body prevents reconstruction of the prompt.

evidence.quote: have bred all these varieties from the same set of eggs, so that there can be no doubt that they are all the same species?

record_reviews.summary: This is a 91-block institutional diploma, not a personal letter. The Latin text enrolls Charles Darwin among honorary members of the Edinburgh Royal Medical Society, gives the society’s foundation/charter, names the officeholders, and is followed by a full English translation. Although the diploma is dated 1861, the apparatus says transmission occurred in December 1862; both document date and receipt/transmission must remain distinct.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1862-12-11; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: The Society is the issuing institutional voice, with named presidents, secretaries, and fellows signing or appearing in the diploma. No one individual should be treated as the personal incoming correspondent.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The diploma’s 1861 document date and 1862 transmission are later boundary evidence; no 1851–55 reply is established.

evidence.quote: We enroll the most distinguished and most honoured man Charles Darwin among the very foremost of the honorary members of our society

record_reviews.summary: Edmondston answers Darwin’s questions about pigeons: he doubts they feed far from breeding places, says the island birds retain the Rock Dove’s uniform colour, and affirms that drifted trees occur though less often than formerly. He praises Darwin’s work on varieties and mentions Macgillivray as an early scientific friend; the opening and final sentence are incomplete. The Shetland setting and fragment extent constrain the evidence.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1856-05-02; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Laurence Edmondston is the incoming writer; the incomplete opening and closing prevent certainty about the full query or any enclosure, while the Macgillivray reference remains Edmondston’s report.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1856 incoming fragment is just outside 1851–55; it answers an unlocated Darwin query but supplies no current-period link.

evidence.quote: I am delighted to hear you are occupied in the effort to throw light on the interesting & difficult subject of Varieties of Species

record_reviews.summary: Darwin says he has read Espinas’s work but has no particular comment, praises the breadth of research, and then identifies a substantive disagreement: because Espinas scarcely admits evolution, they approach the subject differently. Darwin corrects Espinas’s page-47 representation of his view of ant aphid-farming, explaining that he discussed whether aphids benefit from giving ants their secretion and should also have mentioned defence from enemies. The manuscript is a draft reply to a later book, not an incoming Espinas body.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1809-01-01 to 1877-06-30; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: C. R. Darwin is the outgoing writer to Espinas; Espinas’s book and the page-47 claim are quoted/reported inputs, while Darwin’s marginal notes and the library copy remain separate apparatus.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The 1877 draft responds to Espinas’s later publication; it cannot establish 1851–55 knowledge or a period prompt.

evidence.quote: Allow me to point out that you have unintentionally misrepresented me at p. 47.

record_reviews.summary: Wedgwood reports that the Darwins' Beagle manuscript was read aloud and found varied, engaging, and publishable, while the lagoon-island theory needed clearer explanation. He says little was marked for revision and asks Darwin to remember him to Henslow. This is 1836 manuscript feedback retained for identity/chronology context only.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1836-12-20 to 1836-12-20; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Hensleigh Wedgwood is the incoming reviewer of Darwin’s manuscript; the manuscript and Dr Holland’s opinion are reported objects, not voices.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: 1836 context only; no new 1851–55 relationship.

evidence.quote: I think that of New Holland to which you called my attention is well worth insertion.

record_reviews.summary: Wedgwood gives Darwin an urgent family medical report about his father’s fluctuating illness, Elizabeth’s anxiety, and a letter that may have gone to Down. He apologizes for hurried news and explains the special parcel routing. The source is family/medical context from 1842, with no scientific prompt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1842-09-25 to 1842-09-25; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Hensleigh Wedgwood is the incoming family writer; quoted questions and reported family speech remain within his account.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: 1842 context only; no later-period relationship.

evidence.quote: I am very sorry I wrote in such an excessively hurried manner to you

record_reviews.summary: The Ray Society council minute records a request that Darwin agree to publish Living Cirripedia in parts, beginning with pedunculated cirripedes and their illustrations. The original correspondence is missing; this one-block minute establishes a request and administrative route, not its exact wording or receipt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Original XML bound 1850-11-04 to 1850-11-06; this boundary probe is not period-eligible. Broad bounds are retained without assigning an exact day.

issues.assessment: Targets span the 1850s–70s and contexts 1836–50; XML open lower bounds of 1809 are metadata artifacts and do not establish 1851–55 inclusion.
Ray Society and Edinburgh Royal Medical Society records retain institutional authorship; no secretary or member is substituted as an individual sender.
Later Darwin bodies were checked for explicit use/forwarding, but no preserved witness provides a period-specific relationship for these records.

issues.description: Replaced batch-64 generic summaries with source-specific accounts. Corrected minutes replacing missing Darwin letters (4654/4744F), linguistic analogy (2070), moral-instinct critique and Darwin notes (7470), 23-block errata (5827), 91-block institutional diploma and separate 1861/1862 dates (3853F), and 1856/1857 later boundary leads (2032/1865).
